blocks.text: It is remarkable that Rashi places the leaping legs at the neck of the locust, whereas, as is well known, the grasping legs are in front and the leaping legs behind; Reggio commits the same error (in his edition of the Pentateuch, Lev. 11, 21); by contrast, the Zunz Bible correctly translates the words of the text אשר (לא) לו כרעים ממעל לרגליו as: “which has joints above the hind legs”, by which the actual leaping legs are meant.

Hence the appearance of the גובאי is mentioned as a plague upon the land (Sota 49b); likewise the Jerusalem Talmud (Berachoth C. 6, fol. 10, c) ordains that at the sight of the גוביי the blessing ברוך דיין האמת be recited.
The Jerusalem Talmud (Sabbat 12b) speaks of the healing power of the צפורת כרמים thus: אשה סטיפה מושחת ממנה והיא מחרפא; this presupposes that the insect is fatty.

Of a poem composed in the Middle Ages (by שלמה דפיירה), which Dukes partly reproduces in Ozar Nechmad vol. 2, p. 110, the first two strophes read: כרגע נקבצו מקרים ובאו בדי ארבה וצפורת כרמים ישיבו לכל יקר ופאר לאפר ומכל עץ פרי עושים פחמים, from which it emerges that צפורת כרמים was regarded as a voracious locust.
And thus our insect says in the Perek Schire (ch. 4) אשא עיני אל ההרים etc., where its abode on the mountains is surely in mind.
Cf. Bartenoro on Schekalim 6, 3.

Perhaps the following speaks for this view: שושיבא may be related to שושיפא; this word means cloak, covering, and indeed the citron-leaf-like wings of the mantis sometimes wrap somewhat around the body, just as the covering wings in general are very broad and deceptively resemble that kind of leaf.
Buxdorf Lex. p. 2058 needlessly explains it as snail.

In several words derived from Greek and Latin the μ [m] was lost, e.g. כרבלין (rattle, κρέμβαλον [krembalon]), קפנדריא (short way, compendiaria); thus also מוף corresponds to Memphis; חוף, τύμπανον [tympanon]; סבכא, σαμβύκη [sambykē] etc. — By contrast, in Aramaic words ν [n] is often inserted as ם, e.g. קומקמא (kettle, cucuma, κουκκούμιον [koukkoumion]), פרמביא (halter, φορβεία [phorbeia]), סימפין, tube, σίφων [siphōn]).

Likewise the Jerusalem Talmud (Tanit C. 3, H. 6 fol. 66, 4) says: למה נקרא שמו חסיל שהוא חוסל את הכל, it is called חסיל “devourer” because it devours everything; Landau (in his Machsor edition (Schachrit of the 7th day of Pesach s.v. חסדי ד' אוכיר) translates the word freely and without justification as “Erdkrebs”, as the mole cricket is otherwise called, which, however, is surely not meant in the Bible and the Talmud. — The חנמל mentioned in the same place is translated by older commentaries on the Machsor, following Rashi (on Ps. 78, 47), as: locust; by Landau as: frost; by Gesenius (in the Wörterb.) as: ant, compounded of נמל with a prefixed ח.

The best-known species belonging to the locust family are enumerated fairly completely in the Piyyut piece אדמה מארר for Hoschana Rabba, namely: חסיל סלעם, צלצל, ארבה, תולעת ילק, גובי, חגב, גזם and חסיל.

In Midr. R. Wajikra fol. 190, col. 1 the expression נשכו עקרב is also found; by contrast, ibid. Bamidbar fol. 240. col. 1. has עקרב מכה בעוקצו, which Ide Mosche erroneously explains as עוקץ לשונו; the stinging segment, as is well known, is located in front of the scorpion's anus. Cf. וביב נושכת בצירעה (Rashi on Chulin 58b) and: עקרבא ליעקציה (Bechoroth 31b). Jeruschalmi (Beracholh 9a) gives as the reason why the scorpion is more dangerous than the snake: דמחייא והורה דמחייא, that it repeats the sting several times.

This single and accidental event is mentioned very frequently in the Midrash in order to show the course of Providence, which makes use of unusual means to seek out and punish the sinner (see Rabba 12b; 127b; 272, c and often).
The Paytan in the German rite (Jozar for the Sabbath of Rosch-Chodesch, s.v. אלהינו אלהים) calls the spiders טויות, “the spinning ones.”

Bechai (Chobbot ha-Lebaholh ed. Fürstenthal p. 240, 2) uses the image of the spider, which spins its web so densely that the light of the sun cannot penetrate it, to designate passion, which obstructs the light of reason.

Geiger translates שממית (following Gesenius) as star lizard and expresses himself thus: “Not as Rashi: he made it so desolate that the spiders made their web there, which is precisely why it is said that he brought them up” (Urschrift und Uebersetzungen der Bibel. p. 68); but the Hiphil העלה in our passage means “to cause to ascend”, see Rashi on Num. 8, 2; in our Talmud passage, therefore, the sense is: Amon caused spiders to climb onto the altar, since he let it fall into desolation.
The manna in the wilderness is said to have been 60 times sweeter than honey (Berachoth 57b), cf. §. 438, last note.
The Midrash (Tanchuma on P. Balak) has the proverb about the hornet: “I want neither your honey nor your sting.”
The Arabic ن [n] is lost in the Aramaic words; thus קפור (§. 134) is the Arabic قُنْفُذ [qunfudh]; חויר (§. 170) خِنْزِير [khinzīr]; עכביש (§. 400), عَنْكَبُوت [ʿankabūt] etc.

In our passage the fat is called חרבא (see §. 92); but actual fat is entirely lacking in insects; thus Aristotle says (Naturg. 7, 7): insects have no fat (πιμελή [pimelē]), as is generally the case with the bloodless (i.e. white-blooded) animals. Plinius repeats the same (h. n. 11, 4, 3); we must therefore understand here by חרבא the juice of the cockchafer, which does indeed feel fatty to the touch.
